quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Synthetic aviation fuel is made from captured carbon dioxide and renewable hydrogen, and it can power existing aircraft without engine changes. Airlines like it because batteries are too heavy for long flights. The fuel is currently several times more expensive than kerosene. Producers say that costs will fall once factories operate at scale. Governments are considering mandates that oblige airlines to blend in a rising share each year. Airlines respond that mandates without matching subsidies will simply raise fares. Environmental groups add that the fuel needs enormous amounts of clean electricity, which may be better used elsewhere.
options: Environmental groups prefer synthetic fuel because it uses very little electricity to produce.
Airlines want mandates without subsidies because higher fares would improve their long-term revenue.
Synthetic fuel could decarbonise long-distance flying and cost, mandates and electricity demand remain disputed.
Synthetic fuel is already cheaper than kerosene, so mandates would cost airlines nothing extra.
quests.correctAnswer: Synthetic fuel could decarbonise long-distance flying and cost, mandates and electricity demand remain disputed.
quests.hint: Imagine each group speaking in turn: producers, airlines, governments, environmental groups. What do they disagree about?
quests.explanation: Every party accepts that the fuel works technically; the argument is about who pays and whether the electricity could be better used. The wrong options reverse the cost, the airlines' position and the groups' concern.
keyPoints: Synthetic fuel can power existing aircraft without engine changes.
It is currently far more expensive, though producers expect costs to fall.
Mandates, fares and the use of clean electricity are contested.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Lithium is essential for the batteries in electric vehicles, and demand is expected to rise sharply. Most of it comes from a few places, including salt flats where brine is pumped to the surface and left to evaporate. Local communities say this uses scarce water in already dry regions. Mining companies reply that they create jobs and pay taxes that fund schools and clinics. New techniques can extract lithium with less water, but they are costly and not yet proven at scale. Governments must therefore weigh the climate benefits of electric transport against harm to fragile places. Some are requiring companies to consult residents before receiving permits.
options: Lithium is found in many countries, so most regions share the burden of extraction.
New extraction techniques are already used at scale and have removed the water problem.
Communities support the mines because the companies use little water in dry regions.
Lithium mining supports electric vehicles and strains local water, forcing governments to weigh trade-offs.
quests.correctAnswer: Lithium mining supports electric vehicles and strains local water, forcing governments to weigh trade-offs.
quests.hint: Rank the ideas: which one explains why governments are hesitating?
quests.explanation: Rising demand and local water stress create a trade-off, and consultation is one attempt to manage it. The wrong options misstate where lithium is found, communities' attitude and the maturity of the new methods.
keyPoints: Electric vehicle batteries need lithium, and demand is rising sharply.
Brine extraction uses water in dry regions, worrying local communities.
Governments weigh climate gains against local harm and require consultation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Inspections are supposed to raise school standards by identifying weaknesses and pressing for improvement. Head teachers often say that the prospect of an inspection changes how the whole school behaves. Lessons become more formal, and teachers spend time preparing paperwork that inspectors might ask to see. Some schools even avoid taking on challenging pupils whose results might lower their rating. Supporters argue that inspection protects children in schools that would otherwise be left to decline. Critics counter that trust and professional freedom produce better teaching than fear of a judgement. A number of countries have therefore moved to lighter, more advisory visits.
options: Inspections improve teaching because head teachers do not change their school's behaviour beforehand.
Inspection can protect standards but distort teaching so lighter visits are spreading.
Most countries have abandoned inspection altogether in favour of unannounced formal assessments.
Supporters believe inspection is unnecessary because trust produces better teaching than judgement.
quests.correctAnswer: Inspection can protect standards but distort teaching so lighter visits are spreading.
quests.hint: Try summarising in a single sentence that contains a benefit, a cost and a response.
quests.explanation: The purpose of inspection is legitimate, but its side effects lead some systems to soften it. The wrong options deny behavioural change, misdescribe the supporters and exaggerate the move away from inspection.
keyPoints: Inspections aim to identify weaknesses and drive improvement.
The prospect of them changes teaching and may discourage taking difficult pupils.
Supporters cite protection, critics cite lost trust, and some countries use lighter visits.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Pension funds hold trillions in shares and bonds, and many now say they want to invest in ways that reduce climate risk. Selling shares in fossil fuel companies is one option, but critics note that this simply transfers ownership to someone else. Another approach is to stay invested and use voting rights to press companies to change. Activists doubt that firms will move quickly without a threat of losing investors. Some funds do both, selling the worst offenders while voting on the rest. Fund managers point out that they have a legal duty to protect members' savings and cannot accept lower returns for political reasons. The debate therefore concerns not only ethics but also which strategy actually shifts corporate behaviour.
options: Selling shares in fossil fuel companies removes the shares from the market and ends the companies' operations.
Fund managers are free to accept lower returns whenever members' savings are used for political goals.
Pension funds disagree over whether selling or engaging with polluters best reduces climate risk.
Activists believe engagement will change companies quickly without a threat of losing investors.
quests.correctAnswer: Pension funds disagree over whether selling or engaging with polluters best reduces climate risk.
quests.hint: Find the question the whole paragraph is really asking.
quests.explanation: The paragraph sets divestment against engagement under the constraint of legal duty, and asks which actually changes behaviour. The wrong options overstate divestment, deny the legal duty and reverse the activists' doubt.
keyPoints: Pension funds want to reduce climate risk in their investments.
Selling shares merely changes ownership, while voting can pressure companies.
Managers must protect savings, so the debate is about effectiveness.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Insurers in fire-prone regions are withdrawing cover or raising premiums sharply. They say that wildfires have become so frequent and destructive that the old pricing models no longer work. Premiums in the worst areas have doubled within three years. Homeowners argue that they are being punished for risks they cannot control, since they cannot move a forest. Some states have created insurers of last resort, which offer basic cover at limited cost, but their reserves would not survive a catastrophic season. Regulators face a dilemma because forcing insurers to stay may bankrupt them, while allowing them to leave may leave communities defenceless. Planners suggest that the long-term answer lies in building fewer homes in the riskiest areas and hardening those that already exist.
options: Wildfire insurance is failing in risky regions, forcing hard choices for regulators and homeowners.
Planners say the best answer is to build more homes in the riskiest areas quickly.
Insurers of last resort have large reserves that could survive a catastrophic wildfire season.
Homeowners accept higher premiums because they can control the risk by moving the forest.
quests.correctAnswer: Wildfire insurance is failing in risky regions, forcing hard choices for regulators and homeowners.
quests.hint: Notice the phrase that describes regulators' position. It captures the heart of the paragraph.
quests.explanation: Insurers, homeowners and regulators each face a constraint, and planners point to longer-term measures. The wrong options reverse the reserves, homeowners' view and planners' advice.
keyPoints: Insurers are leaving or charging more where wildfires are frequent.
Homeowners feel punished, and last-resort insurers have limited reserves.
Regulators are caught between insurer collapse and undefended communities, and planners want fewer homes at risk.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Remote court hearings became common when courtrooms closed, and many lawyers now prefer them for short procedural matters. They save travel time, reduce costs and make it easier for witnesses with caring duties to attend. Judges report that hearings run on schedule more often. However, defendants may find it hard to follow proceedings on a poor connection, and some feel that they are not taken as seriously through a screen. Cross-examining a witness is also more difficult when the lawyer cannot judge body language. Several courts therefore use remote hearings for routine business but insist on in-person trials for serious cases. Reformers want research on whether outcomes differ.
options: Defendants follow proceedings more readily on screens because poor connections are rare.
Remote hearings have replaced trials, including serious cases, because they run to schedule.
Lawyers find cross-examination easier remotely because they judge body language more clearly.
Remote hearings suit routine legal business and serious cases remain in person for fairness reasons.
quests.correctAnswer: Remote hearings suit routine legal business and serious cases remain in person for fairness reasons.
quests.hint: Sort the paragraph into what remote hearings do well and what they do badly, then find the compromise.
quests.explanation: Remote hearings bring efficiency for simple matters, but weaknesses in communication justify in-person trials for important ones. The wrong options overextend the change and reverse defendants' and lawyers' experiences.
keyPoints: Remote hearings save time and costs and often run on schedule.
Poor connections, perceived seriousness and cross-examination difficulty are problems.
Courts use them for routine matters and keep serious trials in person.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Hospitals with more nurses per patient tend to have lower death rates and shorter stays. Studies from several countries support this pattern, and some governments have introduced minimum staffing ratios. Hospital managers respond that budgets are limited and that ratios can force them to close beds or cut other services. Nurses' unions say that unsafe staffing is already driving experienced nurses out of the profession, which makes shortages worse. Some researchers suggest that flexible ratios adjusted to patients' needs might serve better than a rigid number. Others fear that flexibility would be used by managers to justify cuts. The debate hinges on whether safety or financial control should take priority when they conflict.
options: Hospitals with fewer nurses per patient have lower death rates and shorter patient stays.
Unions say staffing levels are already adequate and are attracting experienced nurses back.
Nurse staffing ratios improve safety and cost and rigid limits are disputed among groups.
Managers welcome ratios because they do not force hospitals to close beds or cut services.
quests.correctAnswer: Nurse staffing ratios improve safety and cost and rigid limits are disputed among groups.
quests.hint: Decide which two priorities are in conflict and who stands on each side.
quests.explanation: Evidence links staffing to safety, but cost and design of the rules are disputed. The wrong options reverse the staffing relationship, managers' concern and unions' claim.
keyPoints: More nurses per patient is linked with better outcomes.
Managers worry about cost, and unions say poor staffing drives nurses away.
Researchers debate flexible ratios versus a rigid minimum.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Ships carry around ninety percent of the world's traded goods, and their engines burn some of the dirtiest fuel available. International rules now limit sulphur in marine fuel, which has reduced air pollution near ports. But cleaner fuel costs more, and some operators have installed scrubbers that wash the exhaust and discharge the polluted water into the sea. That merely shifts the problem from air to water. Slower sailing cuts fuel use dramatically, yet customers often demand fast delivery. New technologies, such as wind-assisted sails and ammonia engines, are being tested. Shipping companies say that regulation must be global, or firms will simply avoid the strictest ports.
options: Shipping pollution is falling only partly, since fixes shift harm, so global rules are needed.
Scrubbers remove pollution, so the sulphur limits have solved the problem for oceans and air.
Shipping companies say each port should set its own rules to prevent firms avoiding strict ports.
Customers prefer slow delivery, which is why ships sail at high speed to save fuel.
quests.correctAnswer: Shipping pollution is falling only partly, since fixes shift harm, so global rules are needed.
quests.hint: Watch for a solution that only moves the pollution somewhere else.
quests.explanation: Regulation reduced one kind of pollution, but scrubbers move it, and slower sailing conflicts with demand, so global rules are needed. The wrong options overstate scrubbers, reverse customers' demands and reverse the companies' position.
keyPoints: Shipping carries most world trade and burns dirty fuel.
Sulphur limits cut air pollution, but scrubbers discharge polluted water.
Slow sailing and new technology help, and companies want global rules.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Venice receives millions of day visitors, but many spend little in the city because they arrive by cruise ship or coach and leave by evening. Residents say that crowds make daily life difficult, and the population of the historic centre has fallen steadily. Some residents have also left because holiday lets pushed rents up. The city has introduced an entrance fee for day trippers on peak days, hoping to reduce numbers and raise money. Shop owners fear that the fee will discourage even those who would spend. Supporters point out that tourism which drives out residents destroys the very character that visitors come to see. Early data show fewer visitors on fee days, but it is too soon to judge the long-term effect.
options: Day visitors spend heavily in the city, so shop owners are eager for their numbers to rise.
Venice's day-visitor fee aims to protect residents and character and its effects are unclear.
The fee has already proved that tourism is harmless to residents and local businesses.
Supporters say the fee is unnecessary because residents in the historic centre are increasing.
quests.correctAnswer: Venice's day-visitor fee aims to protect residents and character and its effects are unclear.
quests.hint: Find the issue that the city is trying to solve and then the limits on what can be concluded so far.
quests.explanation: The fee responds to overcrowding and depopulation, but the results are preliminary and businesses fear harm. The wrong options claim proof, reverse visitor spending and reverse the population trend.
keyPoints: Many Venice visitors spend little, while residents suffer from crowds.
A fee for peak-day visitors aims to cut numbers and raise money.
Shops fear losses, and early data are too limited to judge.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Many newspapers now put their best articles behind paywalls. The income helps to pay for reporters, and readers who subscribe tend to be loyal. However, paywalls reduce the number of people who see the reporting, which matters for stories that the public needs to know. Some publishers keep important public-interest stories free, while others rely on donations or membership models. Researchers note that people who cannot afford several subscriptions may turn to free sources of lower quality. Meanwhile, social media platforms distribute news without paying for it. Editors say that the sustainability of quality journalism depends on finding a balance between revenue and reach.
options: Social media platforms pay publishers generously for distributing their news articles to readers.
Paywalls increase the number of people who see important stories and make free sources unnecessary.
Paywalls fund quality journalism and limit its public reach so publishers are experimenting with a balance.
Editors argue that revenue and reach are unrelated, so publishers can ignore audience size.
quests.correctAnswer: Paywalls fund quality journalism and limit its public reach so publishers are experimenting with a balance.
quests.hint: Ask which two goods the paragraph keeps setting against each other.
quests.explanation: Subscriptions support reporting but restrict audience, prompting mixed models. The wrong options reverse paywalls' effect, platform payments and editors' view.
keyPoints: Paywalls generate income and loyal subscribers.
They limit audience, and some readers turn to lower-quality free sources.
Publishers try free public-interest stories, donations and memberships.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Childcare is expensive in many countries, and some parents find that a second income barely covers the cost. Governments have responded with subsidies, tax credits or free hours for young children. Economists note that subsidies can raise employment among mothers and improve children's early learning. But they also raise costs for taxpayers, and, if the supply of places does not increase, they may simply push fees up. Providers say they struggle to hire staff at current wages. Some analysts therefore argue that money should go to raising staff pay and opening new places, rather than only to parents. The best design remains contested.
options: Analysts argue that money should go to parents and not to providers.
Childcare subsidies help families and children but may raise fees unless supply grows.
Subsidies reduce childcare fees because providers can hire staff at current wages readily.
Economists find that childcare subsidies lower mothers' employment but improve early learning.
quests.correctAnswer: Childcare subsidies help families and children but may raise fees unless supply grows.
quests.hint: Trace what happens if demand is boosted but supply is not.
quests.explanation: Subsidies help families but can inflate prices when places are limited, so supply and pay matter too. The wrong options reverse fee effects, employment effects and where analysts think money should go.
keyPoints: Expensive childcare can make a second income barely worthwhile.
Subsidies raise employment and learning but cost taxpayers and may raise fees.
Analysts suggest funding staff pay and new places as well.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Rare earth elements are used in wind turbines, smartphones and military equipment, and most of them are processed in a single country. That concentration gives the country influence over prices and supply. Other governments want to develop their own sources, but building mines and refineries takes years and produces toxic waste. Recycling could recover some of the materials from old devices, though collection is patchy and the process is expensive. Some manufacturers are redesigning products to use fewer rare earths. Analysts warn that diversification is not simply a matter of money, because environmental standards and local opposition slow every new project. The result is a fragile supply chain that is slow to change.
options: Analysts say diversification is a matter of money and progresses quickly once funded.
Recycling recovers rare earths readily because old devices are collected and processed cheaply.
Rare earths are processed in many countries, so governments have little influence over prices.
Rare earth supply is concentrated and diversifying through mining or recycling is slow.
quests.correctAnswer: Rare earth supply is concentrated and diversifying through mining or recycling is slow.
quests.hint: Identify the dependency and then list the routes out of it.
quests.explanation: The material is vital, supply is concentrated, and each alternative faces practical obstacles. The wrong options reverse concentration, recycling ease and analysts' warning.
keyPoints: Rare earths are needed in many technologies but are processed mainly in one country.
New mines are slow and polluting, and recycling is patchy and costly.
Redesign helps, but standards and opposition make diversification slow.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some countries have abolished university tuition fees, arguing that education should be a public good. Students from poorer families benefit because they are no longer deterred by debt. Yet critics observe that graduates go on to earn more, so it may be unfair for all taxpayers to pay for them. In countries without fees, universities may also be short of funds, and class sizes can grow. Some governments limit places or set entrance thresholds to control costs. Supporters reply that a few fee-free systems still achieve high quality by funding institutions consistently. The wider question is who should carry the cost of benefits that are both private and public.
options: Free tuition widens access but raises questions about fairness to taxpayers and how universities are funded.
Critics say graduates earn less than others, so taxpayer funding is clearly fair.
Students from poorer families are more deterred from university once fees are abolished.
Fee-free systems fail to achieve high quality because universities lack consistent funding.
quests.correctAnswer: Free tuition widens access but raises questions about fairness to taxpayers and how universities are funded.
quests.hint: Locate the sentence that states the underlying question of the passage.
quests.explanation: Fee abolition supports access, but the funding and fairness are disputed because education benefits both individuals and society. The wrong options reverse deterrence, graduates' earnings and quality claims.
keyPoints: Some countries have abolished tuition fees as a public good.
Poorer students benefit, but critics question fairness and funding.
Limits on places and consistent funding are used to control costs.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Genetic tests can now reveal an individual's risk of certain diseases and their family connections. Millions of people have sent saliva samples to companies in order to learn about their ancestry. The companies store the data, and some share it with researchers or sell it in anonymised form. Privacy advocates warn that genetic data can seldom be truly anonymous, since relatives' profiles can help to identify someone who never took a test. Police have used public databases to trace suspects through distant cousins. Supporters say that this helps solve serious crimes. The technology raises the question of whether one person can consent for an entire family.
options: Police oppose the use of genetic databases because they cannot trace suspects through relatives.
Genetic testing raises privacy issues that reach relatives who never consented.
People who have taken a test are the ones who can be identified through public databases.
Genetic data are anonymous, so privacy advocates have little cause for concern.
quests.correctAnswer: Genetic testing raises privacy issues that reach relatives who never consented.
quests.hint: Find the idea that the last sentence points to, and check which option contains it.
quests.explanation: Because relatives share DNA, one person's decision to test affects others, which challenges the idea of individual consent. The wrong options reverse anonymity, who can be identified and police behaviour.
keyPoints: Consumers send saliva samples to learn about ancestry and disease risk.
Companies store the data and may share or sell it in anonymised form.
Relatives' data can identify others, raising the issue of family consent.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Biofuels made from crops such as maize and palm oil were once promoted as a clean alternative to petrol. Growing them, however, requires land, and clearing forests to plant crops releases far more carbon than the fuel saves. Some studies find that fuel from cleared peatland can be worse for the climate than petrol. Food prices can also rise when farmland is switched from food to fuel. Later-generation biofuels use waste materials or algae, which avoid these problems, but production remains small and expensive. Some governments have therefore limited the share of crop-based fuel that counts toward their targets. Farmers who had invested in fuel crops object to the change, saying that policy uncertainty makes long-term planning impossible.
options: Crop-based biofuels reduce carbon in most cases because they replace petrol.
Farmers support limits on crop-based fuels because policy changes make long-term planning simpler.
Waste-based biofuels are already produced on a large scale at a low cost.
Crop biofuels can cause more harm than benefit, so policy is shifting.
quests.correctAnswer: Crop biofuels can cause more harm than benefit, so policy is shifting.
quests.hint: Watch how the paragraph revises an early promise and then describes the consequences of that revision.
quests.explanation: The early promise of crop fuels was undermined by land-use effects, so policy has shifted, causing uncertainty for farmers. The wrong options reverse carbon effect, production scale and farmers' reaction.
keyPoints: Biofuels from crops were promoted as a clean petrol alternative.
Land clearing and rising food prices undermine their benefits.
Governments limit them, and farmers object to the uncertainty.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Traffic-light labels on food packaging use red, amber and green to show levels of sugar, fat and salt. Shoppers can compare products at a glance without reading detailed tables. Studies show that people buy fewer high-sugar items when red labels are displayed. Manufacturers dislike the labels because a red mark can damage sales, and some have reformulated recipes to avoid it. Critics argue that the system can mislead, since a food with one red light may still be healthier overall than one with none. Nutritionists reply that no simple label is perfect but that the benefits outweigh the risks. The labels remain voluntary in many countries.
options: Traffic-light labels make shoppers buy more high-sugar items because red marks attract attention.
Manufacturers welcome the labels because red marks improve sales of products containing sugar.
Nutritionists claim the labels are perfect and that simple colour codes carry little risk.
Traffic-light labels help shoppers and push reformulation, though they remain simplified and voluntary.
quests.correctAnswer: Traffic-light labels help shoppers and push reformulation, though they remain simplified and voluntary.
quests.hint: Sort the paragraph into benefit, industry reaction and criticism.
quests.explanation: The labels inform choices and change recipes, but their simplicity leads to some criticism and their voluntary status limits reach. The wrong options reverse the buying effect, manufacturers' reaction and nutritionists' claim.
keyPoints: Colour-coded labels show sugar, fat and salt at a glance.
They reduce purchases of high-sugar items and prompt reformulation.
Critics say they can mislead, and they are voluntary in many places.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: As sea levels rise, some coastal communities face repeated flooding. Governments can build sea walls, but the walls are expensive and eventually need to be raised again. In some places, officials have begun to offer homeowners payments to move inland, a strategy known as managed retreat. It can protect people and restore natural marshes that absorb storm surges. Yet many residents refuse to leave homes where their families have lived for generations. Others worry that payments will not cover the cost of comparable housing elsewhere. Planners say that voluntary schemes offered early are far less painful than emergency evacuations after a disaster.
options: Sea walls are cheap and permanent, so governments rarely consider moving communities inland.
Managed retreat is offered as an alternative to sea walls, but residents resist it.
Residents readily leave their homes because the payments usually cover comparable housing elsewhere.
Planners say emergency evacuations after disasters are less painful than voluntary schemes offered early.
quests.correctAnswer: Managed retreat is offered as an alternative to sea walls, but residents resist it.
quests.hint: Follow the two responses to rising seas and the reasons one is hard to accept.
quests.explanation: Retreat can protect people and land, but emotional ties and financial doubts slow uptake, and planners urge early action. The wrong options reverse wall costs, residents' response and planners' view.
keyPoints: Coastal communities face repeated flooding from rising seas.
Sea walls are costly, so some places pay homeowners to move inland.
Attachment and payment worries hinder it, but early voluntary schemes are gentler.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A handful of technology companies control the platforms through which many businesses reach customers. They can set fees, decide what gets promoted and use data from smaller sellers to develop competing products. Regulators in several countries have opened investigations. Supporters of the companies argue that their scale allows them to offer low prices and convenient services. Critics say that dominance discourages new firms from entering the market. Proposals include forcing the biggest firms to separate their marketplace from their own retail business. Opponents warn that such rules might reduce quality or raise prices for consumers. The question is how to protect competition without harming the benefits that scale brings.
options: Regulators have already forced the biggest firms to separate their marketplaces from retail businesses.
Dominant platforms rarely use seller data, so small businesses face little competitive disadvantage.
Regulators weigh how to curb dominant platforms without losing scale benefits.
Supporters say that dominance encourages new firms to enter the market and benefits consumers.
quests.correctAnswer: Regulators weigh how to curb dominant platforms without losing scale benefits.
quests.hint: Identify the tension the last sentence names, and see how each group relates to it.
quests.explanation: The concerns about market power are set against efficiency and convenience, and separation is proposed but contested. The wrong options deny data use, reverse the entry effect and treat proposals as done.
keyPoints: A few companies control platforms that many businesses depend on.
They may set fees and use sellers' data, but also offer low prices.
Regulators consider separating marketplaces from retail, and opponents fear higher prices.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Drug testing in sport has become more sophisticated, but so have the methods of those who dodge it. Athletes may use substances that are hard to detect or time their use to avoid tests. Some sports store samples for ten years so that they can be re-tested when better methods arrive. That approach has caught several medal winners long after their events. Critics say that stripping medals years later is unfair to clean athletes who never receive their moment on the podium. Others note that the possibility of future detection acts as a deterrent. Anti-doping agencies add that they need independence from the sports they police to be trusted.
options: Anti-doping agencies say they are most trusted when they are controlled by the sports they police.
Athletes cannot avoid tests, so anti-doping methods rarely fail to detect prohibited substances.
Re-testing stored samples deters doping and delays justice for clean athletes who missed the podium.
Re-testing has rarely caught a medal winner because stored samples lose their value over time.
quests.correctAnswer: Re-testing stored samples deters doping and delays justice for clean athletes who missed the podium.
quests.hint: Notice how one solution creates its own complaint.
quests.explanation: Retesting extends the reach of testing and deters cheating, but late sanctions cannot restore lost recognition, and independence keeps trust. The wrong options reverse detection, retesting results and agency independence.
keyPoints: Dodging tests has grown more sophisticated alongside testing.
Stored samples can be re-tested years later, catching medal winners.
Critics cite unfairness to clean athletes, while others see deterrence.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Prescription drugs can cost far more in one country than in another, even though the ingredients are the same. Companies argue that high prices fund research and that only a few new drugs succeed. Governments in some countries negotiate prices as a single buyer, which gives them leverage. Others allow companies to set prices and rely on insurers to negotiate. Patients in high-price countries sometimes travel abroad to buy medicines. Critics of price controls warn that they may cause companies to delay launching new drugs in markets with low prices. Campaigners answer that research is heavily supported by public money, so the public deserves fair prices.
options: Companies argue that low prices fund research because a few new drugs succeed.
Campaigners say research receives little public money, so companies deserve high prices.
Medicines cost about the same in each country because the ingredients are identical.
Drug prices vary widely between countries, and the dispute centres on whether research needs high prices.
quests.correctAnswer: Drug prices vary widely between countries, and the dispute centres on whether research needs high prices.
quests.hint: Match each group with the argument it uses to defend its position.
quests.explanation: Prices differ due to negotiating power, and firms and campaigners disagree about the role of private and public research funding. The wrong options reverse price variation, companies' argument and campaigners' claim.
keyPoints: Drug prices vary between countries, though ingredients are identical.
Single-buyer negotiation gives governments leverage, while others rely on insurers.
Companies cite research costs, and campaigners cite public funding.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Public broadcasters are funded by licence fees or taxes and are expected to serve everyone, not just profitable audiences. They provide news, children's programmes and coverage of local events that commercial channels might ignore. Their news bulletins are often rated among the most trusted in surveys. Critics argue that a compulsory fee is unfair to people who watch little, and that streaming services already offer plenty of choice. Some broadcasters have responded by launching apps and podcasts to reach younger viewers. Yet if they chase popularity too closely, they risk competing with commercial rivals rather than complementing them. Supporters say that a shared national source of trusted information becomes more valuable as online misinformation grows.
options: Streaming services have made public broadcasters unnecessary because misinformation is now rare.
Public broadcasting faces fairness questions and supporters value it as trusted.
Critics argue that a compulsory fee is fair to people who watch little.
Public broadcasters are funded by advertising and therefore serve mainly profitable audiences.
quests.correctAnswer: Public broadcasting faces fairness questions and supporters value it as trusted.
quests.hint: Find the tension between serving everyone and staying relevant.
quests.explanation: Public broadcasters offer content the market might not, but must justify their funding and adapt without imitating commercial rivals. The wrong options reverse funding, need and the critics' fairness claim.
keyPoints: Public broadcasters provide news and programmes that commercial channels may ignore.
Critics question compulsory fees and the need in a streaming age.
Supporters value trusted information as misinformation grows.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some cities have introduced low-emission zones, where the most polluting vehicles must pay a daily charge. Air quality inside the zones has generally improved, and respiratory illness has fallen among nearby residents. Small traders worry about the cost of replacing older vans. Residents just outside the boundary complain that traffic has been pushed onto their streets. Some cities have responded by offering grants to help owners upgrade vehicles and by extending the zone gradually. Research suggests that the largest health gains come from combining the zone with better public transport. Officials stress that the aim is cleaner air, not raising revenue.
options: Air quality inside low-emission zones has worsened, and respiratory illness has increased.
Research shows the largest health gains occur when zones exist without better public transport.
Low-emission zones improve air and shift burdens so support measures are needed.
Residents just outside the boundary benefit because traffic is removed from their streets.
quests.correctAnswer: Low-emission zones improve air and shift burdens so support measures are needed.
quests.hint: Give the gain, the groups who bear the cost and the steps taken to ease it.
quests.explanation: Zones improve health but create costs and displacement, prompting grants and extension, and the greatest benefit comes with transport improvements. The wrong options reverse air quality, effects outside the boundary and the research finding.
keyPoints: Polluting vehicles pay a daily charge in low-emission zones.
Air improves, but small traders and outer residents bear costs.
Grants, gradual extension and better transport increase the benefit.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Donors often prefer that charities keep their overhead costs low, as though administration were a waste. Yet a charity with no spending on staff training, accounting or evaluation may run poorly. Some large charities have argued that they should be judged by results rather than by the percentage spent on overheads. This is harder to measure, since the impact of a programme may take years to appear. A few donors now give unrestricted grants that let charities decide how to spend the money. Reports suggest that organisations receiving such funding become more stable and more creative. Critics remain wary of trusting recipients without tight conditions.
options: Unrestricted grants make organisations less stable, so donors should attach strict conditions.
Judging charities only by low overheads can mislead and some donors now offer flexible funding.
Results are easier to measure than overhead percentages because programmes show impact quickly.
Charities with little spending on administration usually run better than those with sound management.
quests.correctAnswer: Judging charities only by low overheads can mislead and some donors now offer flexible funding.
quests.hint: See how the paragraph challenges a popular rule of thumb and what it proposes in its place.
quests.explanation: Low overheads seem virtuous but can starve essential functions, so results and flexibility are proposed, though they are harder to assess. The wrong options reverse the value of administration, unrestricted grants and how measurable results are.
keyPoints: Donors often want charities to minimise overhead costs.
Too little administration can weaken a charity, and results are hard but important to measure.
Unrestricted grants seem to help, but critics prefer conditions.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Volunteer tourism lets travellers spend a few weeks helping in schools, orphanages or conservation projects abroad. Participants often return feeling changed, and many donate to the causes they saw. Yet researchers have found that short-term volunteers may lack skills and can disrupt children who form attachments and then lose the volunteers. Local workers sometimes lose paid jobs when volunteers do the work for free. Some organisations now require training and longer stays, and they ask what local communities actually need. Others have moved away from placing volunteers with children altogether. The best projects, according to reviewers, are those led by local people and supported by visitors with relevant skills.
options: Local workers benefit from volunteers because unpaid labour creates more paid jobs for them.
Organisations have concluded that volunteers should work with children more and stay for shorter periods.
Short-term volunteers usually have the best skills and improve the lives of children who form attachments.
Volunteer tourism can harm communities unless projects are locally led and use relevant skills.
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteer tourism can harm communities unless projects are locally led and use relevant skills.
quests.hint: Find the gap between volunteers' intentions and their effects, and the remedy.
quests.explanation: Good intentions do not guarantee good outcomes, so projects need local direction and relevant skills. The wrong options reverse skill levels, effects on local jobs and organisations' response.
keyPoints: Travellers volunteer abroad and often feel changed.
Untrained short stays can harm children and displace local workers.
Better projects are locally led and use visitors with relevant skills.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Wolves were reintroduced to a national park after being absent for seventy years. Elk, which had grazed freely, began to avoid open river valleys where they could be ambushed. Willow and aspen trees recovered along the banks, which attracted beavers and songbirds. Ecologists describe this chain of effects as a trophic cascade. Ranchers on the park boundary say that wolves also kill livestock and that compensation schemes are slow. Some scientists caution that the tree recovery has other causes, such as changes in climate and rainfall. The debate shows how hard it is to trace the effects of a single species in a complex ecosystem.
options: Wolf reintroduction seems to reshape ecosystems, and ranchers' losses and doubts make effects contested.
Scientists agree that the recovery of trees is due to the return of the wolves.
Ranchers say compensation schemes are quick and that wolves rarely kill livestock.
Elk grazed more freely in river valleys after wolves returned, allowing willows to recover.
quests.correctAnswer: Wolf reintroduction seems to reshape ecosystems, and ranchers' losses and doubts make effects contested.
quests.hint: Identify the chain of consequences and then the objections to the tidy story.
quests.explanation: The paragraph presents an appealing sequence, then complicates it with costs to ranchers and doubts about causation. The wrong options reverse elk behaviour, scientific agreement and ranchers' experience.
keyPoints: Wolves returned to a park after seventy years.
Elk changed behaviour, and trees, beavers and birds recovered.
Ranchers report losses, and some scientists question the causes.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some cities close central streets to cars for one day each month or year. Cyclists and pedestrians fill the roads, and shops and cafés often report more customers. Air quality improves noticeably for the day, and people say they enjoy seeing their city in a different way. Opponents argue that car-free days inconvenience people who depend on vehicles, such as carers and delivery drivers. They also point out that a single day does not change everyday habits. Supporters agree, but say that the events serve as a low-cost trial of ideas such as pedestrian streets. Where the trial is popular, some cities have made the changes permanent.
options: Opponents say the events are convenient for carers and delivery drivers who depend on vehicles.
Car-free days cause shops and cafés to lose customers, which is why cities end them.
Supporters claim that one car-free day is enough to change residents' everyday habits.
Car-free days offer a low-cost trial of street changes and popular ones sometimes become permanent.
quests.correctAnswer: Car-free days offer a low-cost trial of street changes and popular ones sometimes become permanent.
quests.hint: Decide what supporters really claim for these events, since it is more modest than the opponents suggest.
quests.explanation: Supporters treat the days as an experiment rather than a solution, and success can lead to lasting change. The wrong options reverse business effects, supporters' claim and opponents' argument.
keyPoints: Some cities close central streets to cars for a day.
Air improves and shops may benefit, but drivers and carers are inconvenienced.
Supporters treat it as a trial, and popular schemes may become permanent.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Schools have tried to reduce sugar in children's meals by removing sweetened drinks and limiting desserts. Children often complain at first, and some bring sugary snacks from home. Where staff involve pupils in choosing new recipes, acceptance improves. Cooks say that reducing sugar gradually is more effective than sudden changes, because taste preferences adjust over time. Parents are divided between those who welcome the change and those who think schools should not restrict food. Health researchers point out that school meals are often the main source of nutrition for children from poorer families, which raises the stakes. Early results show fewer sugary items eaten during the school day.
options: Children readily accept new meals, and few bring sugary snacks from home after the change.
Gradual, participatory sugar cuts can shift children's eating habits.
Schools should not restrict food because school meals are rarely important for poorer children.
Sudden sugar reductions work best because children's taste preferences do not change over time.
quests.correctAnswer: Gradual, participatory sugar cuts can shift children's eating habits.
quests.hint: Ask what makes the change succeed and who has the most to gain.
quests.explanation: Involvement and gradual change improve acceptance, and for some children school meals matter most. The wrong options reverse the pace, the importance of school meals and children's reaction.
keyPoints: Schools cut sugary drinks and desserts from meals.
Gradual change and pupil involvement improve acceptance.
School meals matter most for poorer children, and early results are positive.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Patents on seeds allow companies to control who can plant and sell certain crop varieties. Companies say that developing new varieties costs millions, and protection lets them recover the investment. Many farmers, however, have always saved seed from one harvest to plant the next, and some contracts now forbid this. Smallholders in poorer countries say that they cannot afford to buy new seed each year. Some organisations maintain seed banks that share traditional varieties freely, which can be crossbred with commercial ones. Governments must decide how to reward innovation while protecting farmers' traditional rights and biodiversity. The compromises differ widely from country to country.
options: Seed patents reward innovation but challenge farmers' traditional practices so countries strike different balances.
Governments have found a single compromise that protects innovation and farmers in most countries.
Seed banks sell traditional varieties exclusively to companies that develop new patented crops.
Seed patents have little effect on farmers who save seed because contracts allow it.
quests.correctAnswer: Seed patents reward innovation but challenge farmers' traditional practices so countries strike different balances.
quests.hint: Find the two rights in conflict and the middle ground some organisations create.
quests.explanation: Investment protection collides with a long-standing farming practice, and countries differ on how to balance them. The wrong options deny the conflict, reverse seed bank purposes and claim a universal solution.
keyPoints: Patents let companies control who can plant certain crop varieties.
Saving seed is traditional, but some contracts forbid it, and smallholders struggle to buy seed.
Seed banks and varying national rules attempt compromises.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Care homes for people with dementia have traditionally been designed like hospitals, with long corridors and clinical routines. Some newer homes are arranged as small households of ten residents who share a kitchen and living room. Staff help with cooking and daily activities rather than following a strict timetable. Families report that residents seem calmer and are more likely to eat well. Yet the model is more expensive per resident because it requires more staff, and it is difficult for large providers to introduce. Inspectors also worry about safety, since a homely setting can conceal risks. Advocates argue that quality of life is as important as clinical safety.
options: Traditional hospital-style homes make residents calmer and more likely to eat well than small households.
Inspectors welcome the homely setting because it removes the safety risks for residents.
Small-household dementia care improves wellbeing and costs more and raises safety questions for regulators.
The household model is cheaper because it needs fewer staff to follow a strict timetable.
quests.correctAnswer: Small-household dementia care improves wellbeing and costs more and raises safety questions for regulators.
quests.hint: Decide which two values are being balanced against each other.
quests.explanation: The household model improves wellbeing, but higher costs and safety concerns complicate its adoption, and advocates emphasise quality of life. The wrong options reverse calmness, costs and inspectors' view.
keyPoints: Dementia homes have been clinical, with long corridors and rigid routines.
Small households with shared kitchens seem to calm residents and improve eating.
They cost more and raise safety concerns, but advocates value quality of life.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Small rural schools are expensive to run, and some governments have closed them and bused pupils to larger schools. Larger schools can offer more subjects, specialist teachers and better equipment. Yet children may spend two hours a day travelling, which tires them and cuts into homework time. Villages often lose more than a school, since it acts as a meeting place and a reason for young families to stay. Some regions have tried to keep small schools open by sharing teachers between villages through video links. Results are mixed because technology cannot replace a teacher who knows every child. Officials say that decisions must weigh educational range against the survival of communities.
options: Bused pupils gain extra homework time because travel keeps them alert and focused.
Video-link teaching has replaced the need for teachers who know their pupils.
Villages benefit from school closures because young families move away to larger towns.
Closing small rural schools widens choice and costs pupils' time and village life.
quests.correctAnswer: Closing small rural schools widens choice and costs pupils' time and village life.
quests.hint: Pick out the two goods that officials say must be weighed against each other.
quests.explanation: Larger schools offer range, but long journeys and the loss of a village hub are real costs, and technology only partly fills the gap. The wrong options reverse homework time, the role of video links and the effect on villages.
keyPoints: Governments close small rural schools to save money and bus pupils elsewhere.
Larger schools offer more subjects, but journeys are long and villages lose a hub.
Video links help only partly, so officials must weigh range against community survival.
